character_and_relationship_context: Ingrid Lindgren, a woman in her mid-thirties, has a pragmatic, slightly stern expression that softens only when speaking to her mother. She dresses in well-cut, understated clothes—wool blazers, comfortable trousers, leather brogues—practical for overseeing housekeeping and meeting contractors, but the quality reveals inherited taste. Each morning at 6:30 she reviews the previous night’s occupancy reports and breakfast costs on her tablet while her mother slowly eats oatmeal, occasionally repeating a question about the post. Ingrid answers each repetition with the same even tone, never correcting or sighing, but when her mother turns away she makes a quick note—a reminder to reorder hand soap or call the plumber. Her mother has early-stage dementia; Ingrid has reconfigured the hotel’s ground-floor linen closet into a small bedroom with a courtyard view so her mother can wander safely while Ingrid works at the front desk. A night nurse arrives at 9 p.m., allowing Ingrid to attend regional business conferences where she sits in the front row, asking pointed questions about revenue per available room and tax incentives for historic property renovations. She is known for short, precise emails and standing with arms crossed while listening, then leaning forward when making a counteroffer. She inherited a fortune from her grandparents (her grandfather owned a chain of hardware stores in the 1970s) but is eager to prove she can build something of her own. The hotel in Gamla Stan was a deliberate choice; she stayed there once as a child with her mother, and the memory of cobblestones and heavy oak doors felt like a claim on her past. She keeps a spreadsheet of every guest complaint and compliment and has trained staff to offer free glögg to returning visitors. Her competitiveness surfaces most clearly when discussing expansion: she wants a second property within two years, preferably a smaller boutique hotel in Södermalm, and has already walked the property three times and prepared a detailed comparison of renovation costs versus projected yield. In negotiations with contractors she never shows hesitation, even when secretly calculating whether the margin will hold. The tension between her ambition and devotion to her mother is visible in small ways: she never schedules meetings after 8 p.m., and keeps a framed photo of her mother on the office desk next to loan applications. She grew up in a town outside Uppsala, where her father was a high school teacher and her mother a librarian; the inheritance came as a surprise when her grandparents died within a year of each other. She has no siblings, and the responsibility for her mother rests entirely on her. On Sundays she closes the hotel for two hours and takes her mother for a walk along the waterfront, talking softly about the ships and gulls, never mentioning the business. It is the only time she allows herself to stop planning. Ingrid has a cordial but transactional relationship with the soap supplier, who reliably processes orders placed before noon and once delivered a rush order when she forgot last year. She feels a quiet obligation to guests, knowing from complaint logs that missing amenities like soap prompt negative online reviews within hours. Most mornings she uses her tea break to handle small operational tasks, such as restocking printer paper or emailing the gardener; she rarely postpones a task until later unless interrupted by a guest emergency. However, when her mother is unsettled, she has delayed non-urgent orders to stay nearby, trusting staff to manage later.
objective_situation: It is 7:00 AM. Ingrid has just finished her morning review and her mother is settled with a puzzle in the converted linen closet. The night nurse has left. Ingrid usually takes 10 minutes to herself with a cup of tea before the front desk opens at 8. But this morning, she remembers she forgot to order refills for the third-floor bathroom hand soap. The supplier closes at noon. Her mother is calm and content. Ingrid can either order the soap now, using her tea break, or wait until the day's tasks are underway, risking a guest complaint.
state_and_available_memories: Ingrid is slightly fatigued from a restless night, during which her mother woke twice asking about the post, but she feels a mild satisfaction that her mother is now calmly doing a puzzle. She is aware of the quiet in the lobby and the faint smell of brewing tea from the kitchen. She recalls the sight of the empty soap dispenser in suite 7 last Tuesday, because she had to apologize to a guest who complained at checkout, and that memory carries a twinge of irritation. She also recalls a pattern from her grandfather's hardware stores: he always said a small forgotten order snowballed into two angry customers by noon, and he taught her to 'fix the leak before it floods.'
name: Ingrid Lindgren
